sermon:
## Made, Not Random: The Image of God in Genesis 1–2
*Why the doctrine of creation is the ground you stand on when the culture tells you that you are an accident*

**Text:** Genesis 1–2 · **Supporting:** Psalm 8:3–4 · John 1:1–3 · Colossians 1:16 · Genesis 2:7 · Romans 1:25

A generation has been handed a story about itself, and the story is that there is no story. You are a collision of chemicals that learned to worry. You are stardust that briefly imagines it matters. The culture that raised most of us said the words gently — a documentary voice over a slow shot of a nebula — but the content was not gentle. It was a verdict. You are here by accident, you are gone in a moment, and the universe will not notice either. We absorbed that verdict before we could argue with it, and then we wondered why the young cannot get out of bed. Genesis opens against that exact wound. Not with an argument. With a hammer-blow of a sentence.

And do not miss how much rides on the first page of the Bible. Everything the rest of Scripture will say about your worth, your body, your work, your marriage, your neighbor, and your enemy is already decided in these two chapters. Get creation wrong and the whole book collapses into a set of rules from a god who might as easily have made you for nothing. Get it right and you discover that before there was sin to forgive there was a person to love, before there was a fall there was a gift, and the God who saves in chapter three is the God who made and delighted in chapter one. The gospel is not God cleaning up an accident. It is God recovering something He made on purpose and called good.

### I. God Speaks, and There Is Something (Genesis 1:1–25)

The Hebrew does not ease you in. *Bereshit bara Elohim* — "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). No defense of God's existence, no negotiation with the reader's doubt. The text assumes what our age denies, and it assumes it the way you assume the floor.

Then a rhythm begins, and the rhythm is the argument. Ten times God speaks and it is so. The earth in verse 2 is *tohu wabohu* — formless and void, waste and empty, a chaos with no shape and no life. And God does not fight the chaos the way the other creation stories of the Ancient Near East describe it. The Babylonian *Enuma Elish*, written centuries before Moses set this down, has the god Marduk butcher the sea-goddess Tiamat and build the world from her corpse — creation as murder, order wrung out of violence, humanity fashioned from the blood of a slain rebel god to be the slaves of the divine. Genesis will have none of it. God speaks, and the chaos becomes a home. He separates light from dark, water from land, and then He fills what He has framed — sun and moon, fish and birds, cattle and creeping things. Form, then fullness. A house, then a household.

And where the Babylonians made the sun and moon into gods to be feared, Genesis will not even name them. It calls them "the greater light" and "the lesser light" (Genesis 1:16) — two lamps hung by God to keep time, demoted from deities to fixtures. This is quiet polemic. Every culture around Israel worshiped the sky; Genesis puts the sky on a shelf and says the God who made it is the only one worth your fear. The point is not decorative. If the sun is a lamp and not a god, then you were not made to serve it, and neither were you made to serve the powers our own age has learned to worship in its place — the market, the algorithm, the nation, the self. Only the Maker gets your worship, because only the Maker made you.

- **A. The refrain that keeps landing: "and God saw that it was good."** *Tob* — good, fitting, working as designed. Six times before humanity, and the material world is pronounced good by the One who made it. The Greek philosophers would later teach the West to despise matter, to treat the body as a prison. Genesis got there first and said the opposite. The dirt is good. The sea is good. Your body is not a cage. It is a gift, and it was called good before you did a single thing with it.
- **B. The Word was there before the world.** John reaches back and reads Genesis 1 through the face of Christ: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:1–3). The speaking of Genesis 1 has a name. The voice that separated light from dark is the voice that later wept at a tomb.

### II. Made in His Image, Formed from the Dust (Genesis 1:26–2:25)

Six times, "it was good." Then the rhythm breaks. God stops narrating and starts deliberating: "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness" (Genesis 1:26). The word is *tselem* — image, the same word used for a statue a king would plant at the far edge of his empire so that everyone at the border knew whose territory this was, whose rule ran here. That is what you are. A planted image. A living marker that says this ground belongs to God. Not because you are impressive. Because you were placed.

And then, having made humanity in the cosmic register of chapter 1, the text does something tender in chapter 2. It slows down and gets its hands dirty. "Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature" (Genesis 2:7). *Yatsar* — the word for a potter shaping clay. God kneeling in the mud, working with His fingers. You are dust that God bent down to touch. Both things at once, and you need both. Only dust, and you will despair. Only image, and you will play God. Dust and image, and you can finally stand up straight.

- **A. The image is not a trait you can lose by underperforming.** It is not your intelligence, your usefulness, your beauty, or your productivity — every one of which the market can price and the years can take. The image is conferred, not achieved. Which is why the unborn and the demented, the disabled and the dying, carry it in full. "When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?" (Psalm 8:3–4). David looks at the scale of the cosmos and does not conclude that he is nothing. He concludes that he is minded, remembered, held in the attention of God.
- **B. Rest is written into the design.** God finishes and He rests — not from exhaustion but as a crown on the work, hallowing the seventh day. The image-bearer is not first a worker. He is first a son who is given a garden he did not plant. We have inverted this so completely that we now measure human worth in output, and then we medicate the anxiety that inversion produces. The doctrine of creation says your worth was settled before your first accomplishment, and it cannot be raised by your best day or lowered by your worst.

### III. The Weight of Being Made in a Culture of Accident

I have preached the image of God from a pulpit and then walked to my car ranking the people in the parking lot by how useful they were to me. That is the tell. We confess creation on Sunday and practice the accident story on Monday — we treat our children as projects to be optimized, our bodies as brands to be managed, our worth as a score to be defended. The lie does not feel like a lie. It feels like ambition. It feels like realism. It feels like keeping up. It rarely feels like unbelief while you are living it.

Consider what the early church did with this doctrine when the accident story wore Roman clothes. In the ancient world, unwanted infants were left exposed on hillsides to die — a normal, legal, unremarkable practice. The Christians went out and picked them up. The historian Tom Holland, in his 2019 book *Dominion*, traces how this instinct — that a discarded child bears a worth the empire cannot see — was not native to the classical world but flowed directly from the conviction that every human is stamped with the image of God. That is what the doctrine of creation does when it is believed. It bends down into the mud, like God in Genesis 2, and picks up what the world threw away.

- **A. This is the ground under every fight for the vulnerable.** Take away *tselem* and you can still be kind, but your kindness has no floor — it becomes a preference, and preferences shift with power. Only the image gives the poor and the unborn and the enemy a worth that does not depend on your feelings about them. Paul names the alternative exactly: they "worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25). Every ideology that measures people by usefulness has already made that exchange.
- **B. The image is the ground, and Christ is its restoration.** For the image was defaced, not erased — that is chapter 3, and it is next week. But the Word who spoke you into being in Genesis 1 became dust Himself, "the image of the invisible God," in whom "all things were created" (Colossians 1:16), and He came to remake what we broke. The reason you are told a thousand times that you are an accident is that the accident story asks nothing of you and promises nothing to you. The image asks everything and promises more.

Here is the weight of it for the person reading this on a hard Tuesday. If you are made, then your life is addressed to Someone. It is not a private event you must justify to yourself; it is a gift you answer for to the One who gave it. The accident story tells you that you are free because no one made you and no one is watching — and then leaves you alone in a universe that owes you nothing and remembers no one. The doctrine of creation tells you the harder and better thing: you were made on purpose, by a God who called the whole thing good and then knelt in the dirt to shape you with His fingers, and He has not looked away since. You did not earn the image, and you cannot lose it by failing. It was pressed into you before you drew a breath, and it will be there when you draw your last. The Maker who spoke you into being became dust to buy you back. That is not an accident. That is a purpose older than the light.

You bear the image you did not earn.

## The Day It Broke: The Fall and the Refusal to Be a Creature (Genesis 3)
*Sin is not first the breaking of a rule. It is the ambition to stop being made and start being god.*

**Text:** Genesis 3 · **Supporting:** Romans 5:12 · Romans 1:25 · Isaiah 14:13–14 · Genesis 3:15 · 1 John 3:8

We have made sin small. We have shrunk it down to a list of things we did not mean to do — a temper we lost, a bottle we could not leave alone, a screen we should have closed. We keep the accounting because the accounting keeps sin manageable, a debt we can imagine paying down with a better week. Genesis 3 will not let us keep the ledger. It goes underneath the deeds to the thing the deeds are made of. Before there was a rule broken, there was a creature who refused to be a creature. That refusal is still the engine under every wrong we have ever done, and we are all inside it.

And the modern person feels the truth of this even while denying its name. We no longer say "sin," but we cannot stop diagnosing the thing sin describes — the restlessness that no achievement quiets, the compulsion to prove ourselves that outlives every proof, the way we ruin the good things we are given by needing them to be god. The doctrine of the fall is not a gloomy relic the enlightened have moved past. It is the most accurate account anyone has offered of why a species with every advantage keeps tearing itself apart. Genesis names what our therapists circle and our news confirms. Something is wrong with us, it is wrong all the way down, and it started the moment a creature decided to be its own god.

### I. The Serpent Reframes God (Genesis 3:1–6)

The tempter does not open with a command to disobey. He opens with a question that rearranges the furniture of the mind: "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?" (Genesis 3:1). Notice the distortion. God had said the opposite — eat of *every* tree but one, a garden of yes with a single no. The serpent recasts a generous Father as a stingy withholder, an authority whose limits exist to keep you small. Once the woman is arguing about the rule, she has already lost the relationship. The reframe was the whole attack.

Then comes the promise, and it is the oldest promise on earth: "You will not surely die. For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil" (Genesis 3:4–5). *Like God.* There it is. Not "you will get a piece of fruit" but "you will get out from under Him." The Hebrew for the tree is the knowledge of *tob wa-ra*, good and evil — a merism, the whole range, the authority to decide for yourself what is good and what is evil rather than receive it from the One who is good. That is the fruit. Autonomy. The right to author the moral universe from the inside of your own desire.

- **A. Sin is a theology before it is a behavior.** Augustine, in the *Confessions* around 397 AD, examined his own boyhood theft of pears he did not even want and found underneath it something that wanted the sheer thrill of doing what was forbidden — the will asserting itself against the order of things for no gain but the assertion. He named the mechanism the West would keep rediscovering: the sin under the sins is the self curved in on itself, *incurvatus in se*, the creature who will be his own god. Read that against Genesis 3 and the whole chapter clicks into focus. The forbidden tree was not withheld because the fruit was poison. It was the one boundary that kept the creature a creature — the single point at which the man and woman had to acknowledge that there was a good they did not get to define, a "no" spoken by Someone above them. To eat was not merely to disobey a rule. It was to declare the boundary illegitimate, to insist that no authority outside the self may draw the line. That is why every sin, however small it looks, carries the whole rebellion inside it. Each one is a small vote for a world with no God but me.
- **B. "So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food..."** (Genesis 3:6). The good gifts of creation are turned into the instruments of rebellion. Nothing evil was created. The fruit was good, the desire for wisdom was good, the beauty was real. Sin does not invent new material. It takes what God called good and bends it away from Him. This is why sin is so hard to see in ourselves. It never wears its own face. It borrows the face of something good — a legitimate hunger, a real need, a genuine longing — and rides it one inch past the boundary God set. The woman was not tempted by something ugly. She was tempted by fruit that looked good, promised wisdom, and appeared to be exactly what a person ought to want. The oldest lie does not ask you to love something evil. It asks you to love a good thing more than God, and to take it on your own terms rather than His.

### II. The Break Runs in Every Direction (Genesis 3:7–24)

The eyes open, and the promised godhood turns out to be shame. "Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths" (Genesis 3:7). The first human project after the fall is a cover-up. The first religion is a fig leaf — self-made covering for a self-inflicted exposure. We have been sewing ever since.

Then the relationships shatter in sequence, and the sequence is the doctrine of sin in miniature. Man hides from God — the vertical break. Man blames the woman and, underneath her, blames God who gave her — "the woman whom *you* gave to be with me" (Genesis 3:12) — the relational break. The ground itself is cursed and will fight the man who works it — the cosmic break. Paul reads the whole catastrophe in one sentence: "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). Not a private stumble. A gate through which death walked into the world.

- **A. The exchange has a name.** This is the same swap Paul names in Romans 1:25 — they "worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator." Every idol since Eden is a version of the garden's original move: refuse to receive your life as a gift, seize it as a possession, become the god of your own small kingdom. Isaiah hears the same voice behind a fallen king: "I will ascend to heaven... I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:13–14). *Like the Most High.* The serpent's pitch, quoted back centuries later.
- **B. God comes down still asking.** "Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9). He is not lost; the man is. It is the first question in the Bible spoken to a sinner, and it is a summons, not an ambush. Grace is already moving before judgment finishes speaking. God clothes them Himself — "the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them" (Genesis 3:21). Something died to cover them. The fig leaves would not do. The first death in Scripture is a substitute, and it happens so God can dress the guilty with His own hands. Look closely at the order of the chapter. The man and woman make their own covering first, in verse 7, sewing fig leaves. God does not accept it. Then, after the sentence is pronounced, God makes a covering that costs a life, in verse 21, and puts it on them Himself. Two coverings — one self-made and refused, one God-made and given at the cost of blood. The whole Bible lives in the gap between those two verses. Every religion of human effort is a fig leaf. The gospel is a garment of skins God provides Himself, over the objections of people who would rather cover their own shame.

### III. The Grasp We Are Still Making

I have stood in a counseling office across from a man whose marriage was ending, and I have watched him do Genesis 3 in real time — hide, then blame his wife, then, when that ran out, quietly blame God for the wife he was given. I have done it myself in my own kitchen. The refusal to be a creature is not a doctrine I observe in others. It is the water I swim in. I want to set the terms. I want to decide what is good. I want the garden without the Gardener, the gifts without the giver, the life without the lordship. That wanting rarely announces itself as rebellion. It feels like freedom. It feels like maturity. It feels like finally running my own life.

The modern West did not abandon the serpent's promise. It systematized it. The philosopher Charles Taylor, in his 2007 book *A Secular Age*, describes the slow shift into what he calls the "buffered self" — a self sealed off from any authority outside its own borders, sovereign over its own meaning, answerable to no order it did not choose. That is Genesis 3 turned into a civilization. "You will be like God, knowing good and evil" became a cultural birthright. And the buffered self, having achieved the autonomy the serpent promised, discovered exactly what Adam discovered behind the fig leaves — that a god accountable to no one is a very lonely and very frightened thing.

- **A. The grasp cannot be undone by grasping harder.** You cannot claw your way back into the garden. Every self-improvement program that promises you can is fig leaves with better branding. The exposure Genesis names is not fixed by more effort; it is covered only by a death you did not die.
- **B. Which is why the chapter does not end in despair.** In the middle of the curse, God speaks to the serpent a promise the church has called the *protoevangelium*, the first gospel: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel" (Genesis 3:15). An offspring of the woman will come, and He will crush the serpent, and it will cost Him. "The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:8). The heel that would be struck was nailed to a cross. The grasp of Eden is undone by a hand that refused to grasp — that "did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped" but became a creature to save the creatures who would not be creatures.

Every wrong began with one grasp.

## Judgment and the Ark: Where Wrath and Mercy Meet in One Door (Genesis 6–9)
*The flood is not a children's story with cheerful animals. It is the most honest thing the Bible says about how God feels toward evil — and the door He builds to save us from it.*

**Text:** Genesis 6–9 · **Supporting:** 1 Peter 3:20–21 · Matthew 24:37–39 · Hebrews 11:7 · 2 Peter 3:9 · Genesis 6:8

We put the flood on nursery walls. Smiling giraffes, a rainbow, a boat like a bathtub toy. It may be the strangest thing the church has done with a text — to take the account of near-total judgment and turn it into décor for the room where our infants sleep. Genesis 6 through 9 is not gentle. It is God looking at what human beings had made of the good world and grieving to the point of undoing it. And if you cannot feel the weight of the judgment, you will never feel the wonder of the door. The two are the same story. The flood and the ark are not opposites. They meet at one plank of wood.

We soften the flood because we have quietly decided that a God who judges is a God we would rather not have. The modern instinct is that love and wrath are opposites — that the more loving God becomes, the less He will ever oppose. So we keep the rainbow and lose the rain, keep the mercy and lose the meaning of it. But mercy that is not rescuing you from anything is not mercy. It is sentiment. The door of the ark only matters because the flood outside it is real. Cut the judgment and you have not made God kinder. You have made His grace pointless, a lifeboat launched onto a calm sea, a rescue from nothing at all.

### I. God Sees, and God Grieves (Genesis 6:1–7)

The verdict is total and it is specific: "The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5). *Every. Only. Continually.* This is not a bad neighborhood. It is a diagnosis of the species. The heart — *lev*, the seat of thought and will — has become a factory that produces evil the way a spring produces water.

And then the text says something that should stop us cold. "And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6). *Nacham* — grieved, pained, sorry. This is not a distant deity flicking away an experiment. This is a Father heartbroken over children who have ruined themselves. The judgment of God in this story does not run on rage. It runs on grief. He is not itching to destroy. He is wounded that it has come to this. Get that wrong and the whole flood curdles into cruelty. Get it right and you see a God who takes evil seriously precisely because He takes His creatures seriously.

- **A. Judgment is what love does when it refuses to call evil good.** A God who shrugged at the violence filling the earth (Genesis 6:11 — "the earth was filled with violence") would not be more loving. He would be less. The parent who watches a child's cruelty and feels nothing does not love more; he loves less. The wrath of God is not the opposite of His love. It is His love in the presence of what destroys what He loves. We have inherited a culture that treats the very idea of divine judgment as beneath a decent God — as though wrath were a primitive attribute a mature deity would have outgrown. But run that instinct to its end. A God with no wrath is a God with no love, because love that will not oppose what harms the beloved is not love, it is indifference wearing a kind face. The people asking God to stop judging are, without seeing it, asking Him to stop caring what happens to the world.
- **B. "But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD"** (Genesis 6:8). *Chen* — grace, favor, unearned kindness. It is the first time the word grace appears in the Bible, and it appears in the middle of the account of wrath. Before Noah is called righteous, he is shown favor. The order matters. Grace comes first, and then a life that walks with God follows from it, never the other way around.

### II. God Provides the Door (Genesis 6:8–8:22)

Grace is not sentimental. It gets specific, and it takes the shape of a command with dimensions. God tells Noah to build — cypress wood, three hundred cubits long, pitched inside and out, with rooms and a roof and one door in the side. The word for the pitch that seals the ark, *kopher*, shares a root with *kippur* — atonement, covering. The very thing that keeps the waters of judgment out is a covering. The ark floats because it is covered. So do we.

And notice: there is one door. Not a door on every side, not one for the righteous and a different one for the almost-good-enough. One door, and everyone who is saved goes through the same door — Noah and his sons and the animals, the strong and the weak, all of them through the single opening in the side. "Then the LORD shut him in" (Genesis 7:16). God closes the door Himself. The safety of the saved does not depend on Noah's grip on the latch. It depends on the hand of God on the door.

- **A. The flood is real judgment, not a metaphor.** "The waters prevailed... and all flesh died that moved on the earth" (Genesis 7:21). Hebrews will not soften it: "By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith" (Hebrews 11:7). The ark was a hundred-and-twenty-year sermon in cypress wood. Every plank preached that judgment was coming and mercy had made a way. Picture the neighbors. For over a century they watched a man build a boat the size of a small stadium on dry ground, far from any sea, warning of a flood no one had ever seen. He was a spectacle, a joke, the odd old man with the wood and the animals. And the strangeness of his obedience was itself the mercy — a warning that stood in plain sight for four generations, giving everyone who passed it the same offer Noah had taken. The flood, when it came, did not surprise a world that had been warned. It came upon a world that had watched the warning being built and had decided it would not rain.
- **B. Then, out of the flood, a new world and a promise hung in the sky.** God remembers Noah, the waters recede, and the first thing off the ark is worship — Noah builds an altar. And God binds Himself with a covenant and a sign: "I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth" (Genesis 9:13). The rainbow is a warrior's bow, and it is hung facing up, unstrung, pointed away from the earth. The weapon of judgment is retired into a promise of patience.

### III. The Door That Is Still Open

Jesus reached back to this account when He described His own return: "For as were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man" (Matthew 24:37–39). Notice what He identifies as the sin of that generation. Not spectacular wickedness. Ordinary distraction. Eating, drinking, marrying — good things, all of them — pursued as if the reckoning would never come. That is the more searching indictment, because it is ours.

I preach warning and then live as though I have all the time in the world. I tell you judgment is real and then organize my week as if it is not. The days of Noah were not marked chiefly by monstrous evil but by comfortable inattention, and I am fluent in comfortable inattention. Peter tells us why the door has stayed open this long, and it is not because God has softened on evil: "The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). The delay is not indifference. It is the same grief from Genesis 6, still holding the door.

- **A. Peter tells us the ark was pointing at something all along.** "In the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water. Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you... through the resurrection of Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 3:20–21). The flood is a picture of the judgment we deserve, and the ark is a picture of the One who takes us through it — down into the water of death and up into a new world on the other side.
- **B. There is one door, and He named Himself the door.** "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved" (John 10:9). On the cross, the judgment did not pass over the ark. It fell on it. Christ is the ark who took the flood into His own body so that everyone inside Him comes through dry. The waters that should have drowned us broke over Him instead. And the door in His side is still open.

Hear where that leaves you. The offense of the flood — that God would judge — is answered by the wonder of the cross — that God would be judged. The wrath that filled the sky in Noah's day did not evaporate; it fell, finally, on the head of the Son who built no ark for Himself. He climbed into the flood on purpose. He let the waters close over Him so they would not close over you. That is why the exclusivity of the one door, which our age hears as cruelty, is in fact the deepest mercy — because if there were many doors, God would have had to provide many arks, and there was only ever one Son to give. The door is narrow because the love that made it is costly. And it has not been shut. The same hand that closed the ark on Noah is still holding this one open, and the invitation is not "prove you deserve to come in." It is "come in before the rain."

There is room in the ark.

## The Call of Abram: God's Plan for the World Runs Through One Undeserving Man (Genesis 12)
*Grace does not wait for you to become the kind of person it would make sense to bless. It starts with a word and a promise to someone with no reason to expect either.*

**Text:** Genesis 12 · **Supporting:** Genesis 15:6 · Galatians 3:8 · Galatians 3:14 · Romans 4:20–21 · Hebrews 11:8

For eleven chapters, Genesis has been a widening ruin. A garden lost, a brother murdered, a world drowned, a tower raised in defiance and a people scattered from it. The story of humanity building upward and away from God ends at Babel with a confusion of tongues and a species divided against itself. And then, into that scattering, comes a single word. God turns from the nations in general to one man in particular. The plan to heal the whole world begins not with a program or an army but with a call to a seventy-five-year-old man in a pagan city who has done nothing to earn it. That is how grace works. It always has.

### I. God Calls Before Abram Has Done Anything (Genesis 12:1–3)

The call is pure initiative. "Now the LORD said to Abram, 'Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you'" (Genesis 12:1). Everything Abram is told to leave is a source of security in the ancient world — land, clan, and father's house are your identity, your inheritance, your insurance. God asks him to walk away from all three toward a destination that is not even named. "The land that I will show you." Not "here is the map." Just, "go, and I will show you." Faith is asked to move before it is given the coordinates.

And Abram had no résumé that recommended him. Joshua would later tell Israel the unflattering truth about their founding father: "Long ago, your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates, Terah, the father of Abraham... and they served other gods" (Joshua 24:2). Abram was an idolater from a family of idolaters. There is no hint that he was seeking the true God. God sought him. The choosing runs entirely one direction, and it runs downhill, from grace to a man who did nothing to deserve being found.

- **A. The promise is sevenfold, and it is staggering.** "I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:2–3). Land, nation, name, blessing — and then the hinge on which the whole Bible turns: *all the families of the earth*. The scattered nations of Babel will be gathered again, and the gathering will come through this one man's line.
- **B. Notice the direction of the name.** At Babel, the people said, "let us make a name for ourselves" (Genesis 11:4). Here God says, "I will make your name great." The difference between Babel and Abram is the difference between seizing a name and receiving one. The whole book has been about people grasping for godhood. Now grace hands a man everything he tried to seize — as a gift he could only receive. And the timing is the sermon. The call of Abram comes immediately after Babel, the low point of the primeval history, the moment the human project collapses into a scattered, babbling ruin. It is precisely there — not after humanity cleans itself up, but in the wreckage of its worst failure — that God begins His rescue. Grace does not wait for the ground to improve. It plants a promise in the rubble. The eleven chapters of descent were not the end of the story. They were the dark backdrop against which one word of grace would look like exactly what it is.

### II. Faith That Walks and Faith That Wobbles (Genesis 12:4–20)

"So Abram went, as the LORD had told him" (Genesis 12:4). Four words carry the weight of a life. Hebrews holds this up as the definition of faith: "By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going" (Hebrews 11:8). He went out not knowing. That is faith — not the absence of uncertainty but obedience in the middle of it. He builds altars as he goes, marking the land with worship, calling on the name of the LORD in a country full of other gods.

And then, before the ink is dry on the promise, Abram fails. A famine drives him to Egypt, and fear drives him to lie — he tells Sarai to say she is his sister, so that Pharaoh takes her into his house and Abram is spared and enriched. The father of faith, chapters after his glorious call, trades his wife for his own safety. The text does not hide it or excuse it. And this is the mercy of it: the man God chose to bless the world is shown to us with the fear and the failure fully visible, so that we cannot mistake the promise for a reward he had earned.

- **A. Justification comes by faith, not by performance.** Three chapters later the whole logic of the Bible is compressed into one line: "And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). *Chashab* — counted, reckoned, credited. Righteousness is not produced by Abram; it is credited to him because he trusts the One who promised. Paul builds Romans and Galatians on this single verse. Abram is right with God by believing, and his believing includes the Egyptian failure inside the same life. Grace was never a wage. This is the hinge the whole Reformation turned on, and it is older than Moses. Abram is not declared righteous because he obeyed flawlessly — the chapter that shows his faith counting for righteousness is bracketed by chapters that show him lying about his wife twice and taking Hagar to force the promise along. He is declared righteous because he trusted the God who makes promises to people who cannot keep their end. If Abram had to earn the covenant by his performance, the covenant died in Egypt. It did not die, because it never ran on his performance. It ran on the faithfulness of the God who swore it.
- **B. The faith that matters is not the faith that never wobbles.** Paul describes it: "No distrust made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised" (Romans 4:20–21). Read against Genesis 12, that is not a claim that Abram never faltered — he faltered badly here and again in chapter 20. It is a claim about where his life finally rested. Faith is not a flawless record. It is a direction of trust that survives its own failures.

### III. Blessed to Be a Blessing in a World That Blesses Itself

Here is where the mirror turns. We love the front half of the promise — "I will bless you" — and we quietly amputate the back half — "so that you will be a blessing... in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed." We have built a version of the faith that ends at our own comfort. God blesses me, my family, my house, and there the sentence stops. But grammatically and theologically, the blessing is never a terminus. It is a conduit. Abram is not blessed so that the blessing can pool in his tent. He is blessed so that it can move through him to the nations.

I have preached this and then run my own ministry as if the blessing terminates on my congregation, my platform, my name — the very thing Babel wanted. The sociologist Robert Bellah, in his 1985 study *Habits of the Heart*, named the American religious instinct with painful accuracy: a faith reduced to private well-being, God enlisted as the sponsor of my personal flourishing, the horizontal claim on the neighbor quietly dropped. That is Abram with the second half of the verse cut off. A blessing that refuses to become a blessing is not the Abrahamic covenant. It is Babel with a Christian accent.

- **A. The nations were always the point.** Paul says the gospel itself was preached in advance to Abram in this promise: "And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, 'In you shall all the nations be blessed'" (Galatians 3:8). When you read Genesis 12:3, you are reading the mission of the church three thousand years before it had a name. Every family on earth. That was the plan from the first call.
- **B. The blessing runs through one man to reach us all — and that Man is Christ.** "In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" finds its yes in one descendant of Abram. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law... so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles" (Galatians 3:13–14). You are here, reading this, a Gentile grafted into a promise made to an idolater in Ur, because God kept His word through the true offspring of Abraham who hung on a tree to carry the curse away. You were the "all the families of the earth" the whole time.

So the call of Abram is not an interesting fact about ancient religion. It is your own story told from the far end. The God who found an idolater in Ur and made him the fountainhead of blessing to every nation is the same God who found you — with no more claim on Him than Abram had, worshiping your own set of idols, making your own name — and swept you into a promise older than your birth. And the same word comes to you that came to him: go. Leave the security you have been clutching. Trust the God who will not always show you the map. And do not let the blessing pool in your tent. You were blessed to be a blessing, saved to be a means of salvation to others, grafted into Abraham's promise so that through you the families still outside it might come in. The blessing that stops with you was never the blessing of Abraham. It was Babel with a nicer name.

Blessed to be a blessing.

## The Mountain and the Lamb: God Provides the Sacrifice He Requires (Genesis 22)
*The hardest chapter in Genesis is not first a test of Abraham's obedience. It is the clearest picture, before the cross, of a Father who gives up His only Son.*

**Text:** Genesis 22 · **Supporting:** Hebrews 11:17–19 · John 3:16 · Romans 8:32 · John 1:29 · John 8:56

There is no way to make this chapter comfortable, and we should stop trying. God tells a father to take the son he loves, the son of the promise, the son he waited a hundred years for, up a mountain and put a knife into him. Every instinct in us recoils, and it should. But the recoil is the point. Genesis 22 is meant to bring you to the edge of the unbearable and hold you there, because only from that edge can you see what it cost God to save you. This is not primarily a lesson about doing hard things for God. It is a window into the heart of a God who does the hardest thing for us.

The skeptic reads this chapter and sees a monster — a deity who plays with a father's deepest love and calls it faith. It is a fair objection, and it deserves a real answer, not a dodge. So take it at full strength: a God who genuinely wanted a child sacrificed would be a horror, and any reading that ends with God's appetite for Isaac's blood has misread the chapter completely. But watch where the story actually goes. It goes to a ram in a thicket. It goes to God stopping the very thing He commanded. And it goes, a thousand years later, to a hill outside Jerusalem where God does to His own Son what He would not let Abraham do to Isaac. The chapter that looks like God demanding a father's son turns out to be God rehearsing the day He would give His own.

### I. The Test That Names the Cost (Genesis 22:1–8)

The chapter opens by telling us what Abraham does not know: "After these things God tested Abraham" (Genesis 22:1). *Nasah* — tested, proved, tried. A test is not a trap. It reveals what is already there; it does not manufacture a failure. But Abraham inside the story has no such comfort. He only hears the command, and the command is precise and merciless in its tenderness: "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering" (Genesis 22:2). *Whom you love.* God names the affection before He names the altar. The first appearance of the word "love" in the Bible is a father's love for the son he is being asked to give.

Then the text slows to an unbearable pace. Three days walking. The wood cut and loaded. Abraham lays the wood on Isaac and takes the fire and the knife in his own hand — "so they went both of them together" (Genesis 22:6). And Isaac, no fool, asks the question that hangs over the whole chapter: "Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" (Genesis 22:7). Where is the lamb. Hold that question. The whole Bible is answering it.

- **A. Abraham's answer is either the deepest faith or a desperate hope, and Scripture says it was faith.** "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son" (Genesis 22:8). *Yireh* — God will see to it, God will provide. Hebrews tells us what Abraham was reasoning: "He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back" (Hebrews 11:17–19). Abraham had a promise that ran through Isaac. He concluded that if he had to kill the promise, God would raise the promise. Faith did the math and trusted God past the grave.
- **B. This is not blind obedience. It is trust with a history.** Abraham had watched God bring life out of his own dead body and Sarah's dead womb. He is not obeying a stranger. He is obeying the God who has already done the impossible once, and he reasons that the God who opened a barren womb can open a grave. Faith is not the absence of thought. It is thought that has learned to trust the character of God when the command outruns the understanding. And we should be honest about the offense of the command, not rush past it. God appears here to require a human sacrifice — the very thing the God of Israel would later condemn in the fiercest terms, the abomination of the nations who burned their children to Molech. The chapter holds that horror in front of us on purpose, refusing to release the tension, so that when the ram appears we understand that God provides an alternative to the sacrifice precisely because He never wanted the child. The test was never about God's appetite for Isaac's blood. It was about whether Abraham would hold even the son of the promise with an open hand toward the God who gave him. And underneath the whole terrible scene, God is teaching a doctrine He will one day demonstrate in His own flesh: that He Himself will bear the cost He appears to ask of us.

### II. The Ram in the Thicket (Genesis 22:9–19)

They reach the place. The altar is built. The wood is arranged. And then the sentence no reader is ready for: "Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son" (Genesis 22:10). The knife is up. And in that suspended instant the voice breaks in: "Abraham, Abraham!... Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me" (Genesis 22:11–12). *You have not withheld your son.* God will use those exact words about Himself later, and the echo is deliberate.

"And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son" (Genesis 22:13). *Instead of his son.* Substitution, written in one word. The ram dies in Isaac's place. Isaac walks down the mountain alive because something else went up on the altar in his stead. And Abraham names the place — "The LORD will provide," *YHWH Yireh* — and Moses adds the note that this became a proverb: "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided" (Genesis 22:14).

- **A. Where was the lamb? God provided it.** Isaac asked for a lamb and God provided a ram — but the question was never fully answered on that mountain. Moriah, the tradition holds, is the mountain range where the temple would stand, where lambs would be slaughtered for a thousand years, every one of them still asking Isaac's question. Where is the lamb. The sacrificial system was a mountain repeating the question and never quite answering it.
- **B. The promise is renewed and it reaches to us.** "By myself I have sworn... I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring... and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice" (Genesis 22:16–18). The Abrahamic promise, the one from Genesis 12, is re-sworn at the altar of the given son. The blessing of the nations flows out of a father who did not withhold his son — a foreshadow so exact it should stop your breath.

### III. The Father on the Mountain

For fifteen hundred years Isaac's question stood open. Where is the lamb. Then a man walked out of the wilderness, saw Jesus coming toward him, and pointed: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). John the Baptist finally answers Genesis 22:7. There is the lamb. Not a ram caught by its horns as a stopgap, but the Son Himself, walking to a hill, carrying the wood of His own sacrifice on His own back — as Isaac carried the wood up Moriah — to a place outside Jerusalem, on the ridge of the same mountain range.

And here is the turn that changes how you read the whole chapter. On Moriah, God stopped the knife. On Calvary, no voice from heaven broke in. There was no ram in the thicket for the Son of God. The hand was not stayed. The words God spoke to Abraham — "you have not withheld your son, your only son" — God then spoke over Himself, and Paul says it plainly: "He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?" (Romans 8:32). *Did not spare His own Son.* What God would not require of Abraham, God required of Himself.

- **A. This is why we cannot flatten the chapter into a lesson about our sacrifices.** I have preached Genesis 22 as if the point were how much Abraham was willing to give up for God, and every time I have made that the point I have gotten it backwards. The center of gravity is not the father who lifted the knife and was stopped. It is the Father who lifted the knife and did not stop — because the one on the altar this time was carrying not His own sin but yours and mine. "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son" (John 3:16). *Gave His only Son.* The love that named Isaac in verse 2 became the love that gave the true Son in full.
- **B. Jesus said Abraham saw it coming.** "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad" (John 8:56). On that mountain, in that ram, in that provision, Abraham glimpsed the day the true Lamb would be provided — and he was glad. You stand on the far side of what Abraham only foresaw. The lamb has been provided. The question Isaac asked walking up the hill has a face and a name and a wound in His side.

And this changes what you do with your own Moriah — the thing God seems to be asking you to lay on the altar, the child, the future, the dream, the security you cannot imagine surrendering. The chapter does not promise that God will always send the ram and stay the knife; sometimes the thing is truly laid down and not returned. What the chapter promises is deeper than that. It promises that the God asking you to trust Him with what you love most is a God who has already trusted Himself with the same thing and did not flinch. He knows exactly what the altar costs, because He stood on Calvary and did not come down from it. You are not being asked to prove your love to a God who risks nothing. You are being asked to open your hand to a Father who opened His own — who gave the Son He loved, His only Son, and heard no voice from heaven say stop. The God of Moriah can be trusted with your Isaac, because the God of Calvary already gave His.

God Himself will provide the lamb.

## Meant for Good: Providence in the Ruins of a Family (Genesis 37–50)
*What men intend for evil, God is weaving toward salvation — and He does it without ever excusing the evil or explaining the pain away.*

**Text:** Genesis 37–50 · **Supporting:** Genesis 45:5–8 · Romans 8:28 · Acts 2:23 · Psalm 105:17–19 · Isaiah 55:8–9

The Joseph story is the longest single narrative in Genesis, and it is not a story of a hero. It is a story of a family so broken it should have ended the covenant line — jealousy, attempted murder, a brother sold into slavery, a father deceived into decades of grief, betrayal stacked on betrayal. And running underneath all of it, invisible to every person inside the story while it is happening, is the hand of God. That is the doctrine this whole account exists to teach. Not that God prevents the evil. That God, without ever authoring or excusing the evil, is weaving it — every ugly thread of it — toward a rescue no one could have foreseen.

This is the question that empties pews and ends prayers. Not "does God exist," but "where was He when it happened" — when the diagnosis came, when the child was buried, when the marriage ended, when the years in the prison stacked up and no one came. We can survive a God we cannot prove. What we cannot survive is a God who seems absent in the pit. And Genesis does not answer that question with a philosophy of suffering. It answers it with a life — one man's slow descent into every kind of loss, with a single sentence running quietly underneath it that the man himself could not hear. The answer to "where was God" is not an argument. It is a name, and the name is Joseph, and the sentence underneath his suffering is one we will not be able to read until the very last chapter.

### I. The Pit and the Prison (Genesis 37–40)

It begins with a father's favoritism and a boy's arrogance. Jacob loves Joseph more and dresses him in a coat that announces it. Joseph dreams that his family will bow to him and cannot help telling them. The brothers' hatred hardens until, seeing him coming across a field, they strip him, throw him in a pit, and sell him to traders bound for Egypt — then dip the coat in goat's blood and let their father believe a beast has devoured his son. "All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted" (Genesis 37:35). The covenant family is a crime scene.

And then Joseph's life in Egypt does the opposite of ascend. He is a slave who does everything right in Potiphar's house, is falsely accused by Potiphar's wife when he refuses her, and is thrown into prison for his integrity. He interprets the dreams of two fellow prisoners, asks only to be remembered, and is promptly forgotten — "yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him" (Genesis 40:23). For thirteen years the trajectory is straight down. Betrayed by his brothers, enslaved, framed, imprisoned, and forgotten. If providence is real, it is at this point completely invisible.

- **A. The one refrain the narrator will not let us miss.** In the middle of the descent, four times, the text quietly insists: "The LORD was with Joseph" (Genesis 39:2, 39:21, and around it). Not "the LORD rescued Joseph from these things." The LORD was *with* him — in Potiphar's house, in the prison, in the forgetting. Presence is not the same as rescue, and the text refuses to promise the second while it insists on the first. God with him in the pit is the doctrine, long before God exalts him from it.
- **B. Psalm 105 tells us what the narrative only shows.** Looking back centuries later, Israel sang: "He had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave. His feet were hurt with fetters; his neck was put in a collar of iron; until what he had said came to pass, the word of the LORD tested him" (Psalm 105:17–19). *God sent a man ahead of them.* The selling that the brothers meant as murder, the psalm calls a sending. The same event. Two agents. That is the whole mystery of providence in one sentence. And that psalm was written on the other side of the story, by people who could finally see what Joseph could not see from inside the fetters. This is the ache of providence: it is almost always read backward. The meaning that is obvious to Psalm 105 was invisible to Joseph in the collar of iron. He did not get a footnote in the pit explaining that this was a sending. He got the pit. The interpretation came later, sometimes decades later, sometimes only from the far side of a life. Which means the person who cannot see the meaning of their own suffering right now is not failing to have faith. They are standing exactly where Joseph stood — inside the story, before the psalm.

### II. The Revelation and the Reversal (Genesis 41–47)

The turn, when it comes, is total. Pharaoh dreams, no one can interpret, the cupbearer finally remembers, and in a single day Joseph goes from a dungeon to the second throne of Egypt, set over the food of the known world in a coming famine. And the famine that raises Joseph is the famine that drives his brothers down to Egypt to buy grain — where they bow before a governor they do not recognize, fulfilling to the letter the dream they had tried to murder him for having.

Joseph tests them, weeps behind closed doors, and finally cannot hold it. "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" (Genesis 45:3). And then he says the thing that is the theological center of the entire book, and he says it not to excuse his brothers but to comfort them: "And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life... So it was not you who sent me here, but God" (Genesis 45:5–8). *God sent me.* He does not pretend the brothers were innocent. He does not soften what they did. He simply says that over and underneath their evil, God was doing something else entirely, and God's purpose was the one that held.

- **A. This is not fatalism, and it is not a denial of the evil.** Joseph does not say, "no harm was done" or "it all worked out, so it was fine." The brothers really sinned; the pit was real, the years were real, the grief was real. Joseph holds two truths that a shallower faith cannot hold at once: they meant it for evil, and God meant it for good, and both are fully true of the very same act. The Bible never resolves that tension by dissolving one side of it.
- **B. Grace flows down onto the guilty.** The brothers deserve nothing, and Joseph gives them everything — land, provision, protection, the best of Egypt. The one they wronged becomes the one who saves them. The family that should have died in its own sin is preserved by the mercy of the brother they betrayed. You have read this pattern before. You will read it again on a cross. And notice what providence does not do. It does not tie the pain into a bow. Joseph names his firstborn Manasseh, "for God has made me forget all my hardship" (Genesis 41:51) — and yet the story keeps making him remember, weeping so loudly the Egyptians hear it through the walls. The good God brought did not erase the years in the pit and the prison. It redeemed them without deleting them. That is the honest doctrine of providence, and it is the one that can actually hold a suffering person: not that the wound never happened, not that it was secretly pleasant all along, but that the God who was with Joseph in the dark was working a rescue the whole time that the darkness could not see and could not stop.

### III. Meant for Good, in a World That Wants a Cleaner Story

We want a providence without a pit. We want God to keep the promise by keeping us out of Egypt. And when He does not — when the diagnosis comes back, when the marriage cracks, when the years go by and the dream stays buried — we conclude He has forgotten us, exactly as the cupbearer forgot Joseph. I have sat with people in my office in the thirteenth year of their prison and had no interpretation to offer, and I have been in that prison myself, certain the silence meant abandonment. Genesis 37 through 50 will not give me a formula for reading providence forward. It only insists that the meaning is there before I can see it, the way it was there in the pit while Joseph could see nothing but the sky through the top of a hole.

The great modern temptation is to demand that God's purposes be legible to us in real time — to make His providence pass the bar of our understanding or be dismissed as cruelty. But God said through Isaiah, "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways" (Isaiah 55:8–9). And the New Testament turns Joseph's confession into a promise for every believer: "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28). Not "all things are good." All things *work together*. The pit is not good. The pit is woven.

- **A. The pattern reaches its depth at the cross.** The brothers said it of Joseph without knowing they were prophesying: what you meant for evil, God meant for good. And at the center of history stands the one place where that sentence is most fully and most terribly true. Peter preached it at Pentecost: "This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Acts 2:23). The worst act in human history — the murder of the Son of God — was, in the same instant, the ordained means of the world's salvation. Meant for evil. Meant for good. The cross is Genesis 50 with the whole world in the balance.
- **B. Joseph finally says it plainly to the brothers who still fear him.** After Jacob dies, the brothers panic, certain Joseph has only been waiting to take revenge. And Joseph weeps again and gives them the verdict that ends the book: "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today" (Genesis 50:20). He does not deny their evil. He does not explain the pain away. He tells them the truth that lets them live — that the God who was with him in the pit was, the whole time, keeping many people alive, and them among them.

You meant evil; God meant good.
